clinical: Mastoiditis
Infection can spread from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells, causing pain, swelling and tenderness behind the ear.
Petrous bone fracture
A fracture through the petrous part of the temporal bone can damage the facial nerve and inner ear, causing facial weakness, hearing loss and vertigo.
Otitis externa (swimmer's ear)
Infection or inflammation of the skin lining the ear canal makes the tragus and auricle painful when pressed or when the ear is pulled.
Cauliflower ear
A blow to the auricle can rupture vessels under the perichondrium and form a haematoma. If it is not drained promptly, it can organise into fibrous tissue and permanently deform the cartilage.
Otitis media
Infection of the middle ear, often after a cold, fills the cavity with fluid and pus, which can bulge or perforate the eardrum and cause pain.
Eustachian tube dysfunction

The pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube equalises air pressure in the middle ear with the throat. When it stays blocked, negative pressure pulls the eardrum inward, muffling hearing and causing ear fullness.
Otosclerosis
Abnormal bone remodelling fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, reducing sound transmission and causing progressive conductive hearing loss. Stapedectomy or a prosthesis can improve hearing.
Erosion of the incus (cholesteatoma)
Chronic infection or a cholesteatoma most often erodes the long process of the incus, breaking the chain and causing conductive hearing loss.
Loss of stapedius function
The stapedius is supplied by the facial nerve. If it is paralysed, for example by facial nerve palsy, the stapes is no longer damped and loud sounds become painful (hyperacusis).
Cochlear implant
An implant electrode is threaded through the round window or a small opening into the scala tympani, where it electrically stimulates the spiral ganglion neurons to give useful hearing.
Labyrinthitis
Inflammation of the labyrinth, usually from a viral infection or spread of a middle ear infection, causes vertigo, nausea and sometimes hearing loss.
Ménière disease
Excess endolymph distends the membranous labyrinth (endolymphatic hydrops), causing attacks of vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
Noise-induced hearing loss
Loud noise and ageing damage the hair cells of the spiral organ, outer hair cells first. The damage is usually permanent because mammalian hair cells do not regenerate.
Vestibular schwannoma
A benign Schwann cell tumour, usually on the vestibular nerve in the internal acoustic meatus, causes slowly progressive one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance.
Facial nerve damage
The facial nerve runs through the temporal bone beside the middle ear. Infection, surgery or fracture there can damage it and weaken the face on that side.
GJB2 (connexin 26) deafness

Mutations in GJB2, which encodes connexin 26, are a very common cause of inherited hearing loss. The gap junctions it forms let fibrocytes in the spiral ligament recycle potassium back to the stria vascularis.
Benign positional vertigo (BPPV)
Loose calcium-crystal debris that drifts into a semicircular canal can push on the cupula, causing brief spinning vertigo when the head moves into particular positions.

Inset: macula (magnified).description: The macula is a flat sensory patch in the utricle and saccule that detects head position and linear acceleration. Its hair bundles project into a gel layer weighted with calcium-carbonate crystals (otoconia); gravity or acceleration shifts this layer, bends the hair bundles and signals the brain about head orientation.
clinical: Benign positional vertigo (BPPV)
Otoconia that break free from this patch can drift into a semicircular canal and cause benign positional vertigo, often after head injury or with ageing.

parts.description: Antitragus: the small, rounded tubercle of skin-covered cartilage that lies opposite the tragus, across the intertragic notch and just above the lobule. It is the lower end of the antihelix, the curved ridge that runs parallel to the helix, so the two ridges are continuous. To recognise it, look at the front of the ear: it stands directly opposite the tragus, with the notch between them.

Ceruminous and sebaceous glands of the cartilaginous external meatus: ceruminous glands are modified apocrine sweat glands, with coiled tubules and a myoepithelial layer, and sebaceous glands are holocrine glands that secrete oily sebum. Both open onto the skin surface or into hair follicles of the canal, and their secretions mix with shed keratin to form cerumen. The bony part of the canal has thin skin with no hairs or glands, so these glands are confined to the cartilaginous part.

Tympanic cavity: the air-filled space of the middle ear, a narrow slit in the temporal bone about 15 mm high and only about 2 mm across at the level of the ossicles. It is lined by thin mucosa and contains the ossicles. Its roof is the tegmen tympani, its medial wall the promontory with the oval and round windows, and its anterior wall the opening of the auditory tube. Acute otitis media fills it with pus, and infection can spread upward through the tegmen to the meninges.

Mastoid antrum and air cells: the antrum is a single air-filled chamber behind the epitympanum, joined to it by the aditus, and from it a honeycomb of mucosa-lined air cells extends through the mastoid process. These air spaces are pneumatised (filled with air as they expand) after birth, and chronic otitis in childhood can reduce their development. Infection spreading from the middle ear can fill the cells with pus and cause acute mastoiditis, which pushes the auricle forwards and outwards with tender swelling behind it.

Incudomallear joint: a small synovial saddle joint between the head of the malleus and the body of the incus, the first joint of the ossicular chain. The two bones normally move together as a single lever, but the joint is designed to slip under very large forces, so that an extreme pressure or sound is not transmitted fully to the inner ear. In a dissection, look for it in the attic (epitympanum), where the head of the malleus meets the saddle-shaped facet on the body of the incus.

Superior ligament of the malleus: a short fibrous band running from the head of the malleus up to the roof of the epitympanum (the tegmen tympani). It suspends the malleus from above and helps keep the ossicular chain in its correct position within the attic. In a dissection it is seen as a thin band joining the top of the malleus head to the bony roof of the attic, above the tympanic membrane.

Lateral ligament of the malleus: a short band running from the neck of the malleus outwards to the margin of the notch of Rivinus, the tympanic notch in the scutum above the drum. It lies on the outer side of the ossicle and limits how far the malleus can rotate inwards, so it restrains the chain from being pushed too far medially. In a dissection, it is the band that runs from the neck of the malleus to the upper edge of the drum.

Posterior ligament of the incus: a short band fixing the tip of the short process of the incus to the fossa incudis, a small pit in the posterior wall of the epitympanum. Together with the anterior ligament of the malleus, it defines the axis about which the malleus and incus rotate as one lever when the chain moves. In a dissection, look for it as a short band at the back of the attic, holding the short process of the incus.

Tensor tympani: a small muscle lying in a bony semicanal above the auditory tube, arising from the cartilage of the tube and the adjacent sphenoid bone. Its tendon turns laterally round the cochleariform process, a small bony hook at the front of the semicanal, and inserts on the upper handle of the malleus, so contraction pulls the handle medially and tenses the tympanic membrane. It is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid (a branch of the mandibular nerve, V3) and contracts reflexively with loud sound, chewing and swallowing.

Tensor tympani tendon: the slender tendon of the tensor tympani muscle, which leaves the bony semicanal above the auditory tube and turns sharply outwards round the cochleariform process, a small bony projection at the front of that semicanal. It runs across the tympanic cavity to insert on the upper part of the malleus handle. Its sharp bend round the cochleariform process is the feature to look for when tracing the muscle in dissection.

Stapedius tendon: the slender tendon of the stapedius, the smallest skeletal muscle in the body. It runs from the pyramidal eminence, a small bony bump on the back wall of the middle ear, to the neck of the stapes. The nerve to the stapedius, a branch of the facial nerve, supplies the muscle, and when it contracts it pulls the stapes backwards and tilts the footplate, stiffening the ossicular chain and damping very loud sounds.

Bony labyrinth: the set of hollow bony cavities inside the petrous temporal bone, made up of the vestibule, the three semicircular canals and the cochlea. Its inner surface is lined by periosteum, and it holds the membranous labyrinth, which floats in perilymph, a fluid like extracellular fluid and cerebrospinal fluid (high in sodium, low in potassium). Perilymph connects with the subarachnoid space through the cochlear aqueduct, and pressure waves pass through it from the oval window to the round window.

Scala tympani: the perilymph-filled channel below the basilar membrane, running from the helicotrema down to the round window, where its perilymph meets the air-filled middle ear through a thin membrane. Its basal turn lies next to the round window, so cochlear implant electrode arrays are usually inserted here, through the round window or a small opening beside it, to stimulate the spiral ganglion neurons. Pressure waves travelling along it make the round window membrane bulge outwards, which lets the incompressible perilymph move.

Basilar membrane: the fibrous floor of the cochlear duct, running from the osseous spiral lamina to the spiral ligament and carrying the spiral organ. It is narrow and stiff at the base and wide and floppy at the apex, so a travelling wave set up by sound peaks at a fixed place: high frequencies near the oval window, low frequencies near the helicotrema. This frequency map (tonotopy) is kept up to the auditory cortex, and noise and ageing usually damage the high-frequency basal end first.

Spiral organ (of Corti): the sensory epithelium on the basilar membrane inside the cochlear duct. It holds one row of inner hair cells (about 3500) and three rows of outer hair cells (about 12000), held in place by pillar cells and Deiters' cells, with the tectorial membrane lying above them. When the basilar membrane moves, shearing against the tectorial membrane bends the stereocilia and opens mechanically gated channels; inner hair cells send about 95% of the afferent signal to the brain, and outer hair cells amplify the movement.

Semicircular ducts: the membranous tubes lying against the outer wall of the three bony canals, filled with endolymph and opening at both ends into the utricle. The anterior, posterior and lateral ducts lie in three roughly perpendicular planes and work in push-pull pairs with the matching duct in the other ear. They detect angular (rotational) acceleration: as the head turns, the endolymph lags behind by inertia and deflects the cupula, the gelatinous cap over the crista. Anterior duct: nodding (pitch); posterior: tilting towards the shoulder (roll); lateral: turning (yaw).

Spiral ganglion: the cell bodies of the bipolar cochlear neurons, lying in the spiral (Rosenthal) canal that winds up the modiolus at the root of the osseous spiral lamina. Unlike the pseudounipolar neurons of most sensory ganglia, these cells are bipolar, with a peripheral process to the hair cells and a central process in the cochlear nerve. Cochlear implants stimulate them directly, bypassing lost hair cells, and noise can destroy the synapses between inner hair cells and these neurons before any hair cells die ('hidden hearing loss').

Petrous part of the temporal bone: the dense, pyramid-shaped part of the temporal bone that lies in the base of the skull, between the sphenoid and occipital bones. It forms the medial wall of the middle ear and encloses the inner ear within the otic capsule, which is one of the densest bones in the body. In otosclerosis, abnormal focal bone remodelling around the oval window can fix the stapes and cause conductive hearing loss.

Squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone: the tympanic part forms most of the bony external acoustic meatus, while the squamous part forms the roof of the meatus, the lateral wall of the epitympanum (the scutum) and the roof of the mastoid antrum. The thin tegmen tympani, a part of the petrous bone, is all that separates the middle ear from the temporal lobe and meninges.

keys: Skin of the side of the head
parts.description: Skin of the side of the head: the hair-bearing skin covering the temporal region, lying over the subcutaneous tissue and the temporal fascia. It is continuous with the skin of the auricle and lines the external acoustic meatus. Its sensation comes mainly from the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3), in front and the great auricular nerve (C2-C3) behind the ear.

Subcutaneous tissue of the temporal region: the layer of fat and loose connective tissue lying between the skin and the temporal fascia over the side of the skull. It carries the superficial temporal artery and vein and the auriculotemporal nerve, and it lets the skin slide freely over the deeper tissues. In a dissection it is the fatty layer you reflect to expose the temporal fascia.

Bony wall of the cochlea: the dense bone of the otic capsule that forms the outer shell of the cochlear canal, winding about two and a half turns around the modiolus. Its inner surface is lined by periosteum, to which the spiral ligament attaches, and this ligament holds the membranous cochlear duct against the outer wall. In a histological section it appears as dense compact bone around the perilymph-filled scalae.

Osseous spiral lamina: the bony shelf that projects from the modiolus into the cochlear canal, built of two thin plates of bone with a gap between them. The peripheral processes of the spiral ganglion cells run out through this gap and leave the bone through the openings of the habenula perforata, where they lose their myelin sheath before reaching the hair cells.

Scala tympani: the perilymph-filled channel below the basilar membrane, running from the helicotrema down to the round window. Because it opens at the round window, which lies beside the basal turn, the basal end of the cochlea is the easiest part for a surgeon to reach, and cochlear implant electrodes are threaded into the scala tympani from there to stimulate the spiral ganglion neurons.

Basilar membrane: the fibrous floor of the cochlear duct, running from the osseous spiral lamina to the spiral ligament and carrying the spiral organ. It is narrow and stiff at the base but wide and floppy at the apex, so a travelling wave from the stapes peaks at a place set by frequency: high tones near the base, low tones at the apex. The high-frequency basal region is usually the first to suffer damage from noise and ageing.

Spiral ganglion neurons are the bipolar nerve cells (one process at each end) whose bodies lie in Rosenthal's canal, a spiral channel within the modiolus (the bony central pillar of the cochlea). Each neuron sends a peripheral process through the habenula perforata, tiny holes in the osseous spiral lamina, to contact a hair cell, and a central process that joins the others to form the cochlear nerve. In a cross-section, look for small round cell bodies clustered in the modiolus, close to the base of the spiral lamina.

Cochlear nerve fibres are the peripheral processes of the spiral ganglion neurons, which pass through the habenula perforata (small perforations in the osseous spiral lamina) to reach the hair cells. Type I fibres, about 95% of the total, each supply a single inner hair cell, while type II fibres cross the tunnel of Corti and run along the outer hair cells, each contacting many of them. Inner hair cells therefore supply almost all of the sensory signal to the brain, whereas outer hair cells act mainly as amplifiers.

The wall of the membranous ampulla forms the expanded end of each semicircular duct, made of connective tissue lined on its inner surface by simple squamous epithelium. Dark cells, epithelial cells packed with mitochondria, lie near the crista and secrete potassium into the endolymph, as the stria vascularis does in the cochlea. In a section the lining is thin and flat, except near the crista, where the darker cells stand out.

The cupula is the gelatinous dome that sits on the crista and reaches the roof of the ampulla, sealing it like a swing door. Its density is close to that of endolymph, so it ignores gravity and responds only to the endolymph flow set up when the head turns. When rotation stops, the endolymph keeps moving and bends the cupula the other way, which produces the post-rotatory nystagmus and vertigo tested in Barany's chair. In cupulolithiasis, otoconia stuck to the cupula make it sensitive to gravity.

Type II hair cells of the crista ampullaris are cylindrical receptor cells found mainly on the peripheral parts of the sensory ridge rather than at its crest. Several small, button-like afferent endings (nerve endings that carry signals to the brain) contact each cell, as do efferent endings from the brainstem. Each cell's hair bundle has stereocilia (stiff, hair-like projections) in a staircase, with one kinocilium at the tall edge; bending the bundle towards the kinocilium excites the cell, which signals angular acceleration to the brain.

Supporting cells of the crista ampullaris are the columnar cells that rest on the basement membrane and surround the hair cells, holding them in place. Their nuclei lie in a basal row close to the basement membrane. They are thought to secrete the gelatinous cupula into which the stereocilia project, and they help regulate the ionic environment around the hair cells.

The stereocilia and kinocilium form the hair bundle of each vestibular hair cell in the crista: stereocilia in a staircase of increasing height, plus one true kinocilium beside the tallest row. Bending the bundle towards the kinocilium depolarises the cell and increases firing in the nerve fibre carrying its signal to the brain, while bending it away reduces firing below the resting rate. All bundles in one crista point the same way, so endolymph flowing one way excites the whole crista and flowing the other way inhibits it.

Ampullary nerve fibres are the bundles of afferent axons that carry signals from the crista of each semicircular canal to the brain. The nerves from the anterior and lateral cristae join the superior division of the vestibular nerve, while the posterior crista's nerve joins the inferior division. Within the crista the fine fibres run through the connective tissue core to reach the base of the hair cells, where they form their endings.

The lamina propria of the macula is the layer of loose connective tissue that lies beneath the basement membrane of the macular sensory epithelium in the utricle and saccule. It contains fibroblasts, collagen fibres and small blood vessels, and it carries the macular nerve fibres that climb up to the hair cells. In a section it looks like a thin, pale, fibrous band beneath the epithelium.

The gelatinous layer of the macula is the soft, jelly-like matrix of glycoproteins and proteoglycans that lies directly over the macular hair cells. The stereocilia and kinocilia are embedded in its lower surface, linking the hair bundles to the overlying otoconia. It is thought to be secreted by the supporting cells, and it transmits any shift of the otoconia into bending of the hair bundles.

The otolithic membrane is the weighted, gelatinous sheet that lies over the macula, formed by the gel layer with the otoconia embedded in its upper surface. Because the otoconia weight it, gravity and linear acceleration displace it sideways relative to the sensory epithelium, bending the hair bundles beneath. Its displacement is the stimulus that tells the brain about head tilt and linear motion.

Type I hair cells of the macula are flask-shaped receptor cells, each enclosed at its base by a cup-shaped calyx from an afferent nerve fibre. They are concentrated in the striola, the curved central zone of the macula where the hair bundles reverse their direction. Like their counterparts in the crista, they are more susceptible than type II cells to aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin.

Type II hair cells of the macula are cylindrical receptor cells that lie mainly in the outer, extrastriolar part of the macula, away from the striola. Each is contacted by several small bouton-type afferent endings and by efferent endings from the brainstem. Their hair bundles point in opposite directions on either side of the striola, so the macula as a whole responds to tilt and acceleration in every direction.

Supporting cells of the macula are columnar cells that rest on the basement membrane and sit between the hair cells, anchoring them. Their nuclei lie in a basal row close to the basement membrane. They are thought to secrete the gel that forms the otolithic membrane, which lies over the hair bundles.

Otoconia, also called otoliths ('ear stones'), are small crystals of calcium carbonate in the form of calcite, bound in a protein matrix and embedded in the upper surface of the otolithic membrane. Their mass weights the membrane, so gravity and linear acceleration displace it and bend the hair bundles beneath. When otoconia break loose and drift into a semicircular canal, they cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

The stereocilia and kinocilia of the macula are the hair bundles of its hair cells, with the stereocilia in a staircase of increasing height and one kinocilium beside the tallest row. The bundles on opposite sides of the striola point in opposite directions, so a tilt of the head excites some hair cells and inhibits others, which lets the brain work out the direction of the tilt. Bending a bundle towards its kinocilium depolarises the cell and increases the firing of its afferent fibre.

Macular nerve fibres are the afferent axons that carry signals from the hair cells of the utricle and saccule to the brain. The utricular fibres join the superior division of the vestibular nerve, and the saccular fibres join the inferior division. Their endings are large calyces around type I hair cells and small boutons on type II cells.
